seeds.why: The floor. Three paragraphs of ordinary prose, so a failure here is never about a construct - it is about the path, the font, the page box or the conversion itself, and every other seed in this file can then be read as a difference from this one. A suite whose simplest case fails has nothing to say about its hardest.
seeds.html:
One paragraph of ordinary prose, with nothing in it that any of the four target formats has to think about.

A second paragraph, because the boundary between two of them is a thing a converter can lose on its own, without touching a character of either.

A third, so that the paragraph count this seed asserts is a count and not a pair.

seeds.why: The four character toggles, each on its own word and each with a plain space on both sides. The spaces are the load-bearing part: a converter that mis-attributes the space between two runs changes no visible character and would pass any check that compared only text, so the seed puts a boundary on either side of every toggle. The third paragraph nests one toggle inside another, which is the case a writer tracking a single current style gets wrong.
seeds.html:
Bold italic underline struck normal.

The same four inside a sentence: a bold word, an italic word, an underlined word and a struck word, each with a plain space on both sides of it.

Bold, with italic inside it, and bold again, so that a nested run has to survive as well as a flat one.

seeds.why: Colour twice over, because a run property and a paragraph property look the same on the page and are not the same thing. Highlight is here rather than in the inline seed because it is the one of the two that several formats carry as a fixed palette rather than as a value: a converter that snapped this yellow to the nearest of sixteen named highlights has done something defensible, and this seed is where that gets seen and decided rather than discovered.
seeds.html:
A foreground colour and a highlight and plain text after both of them.

A whole paragraph in a foreground colour, which is the property stated on the paragraph rather than on a run inside it.

Both at once on one run, which is where a format carrying only one of the two has to choose.

seeds.why: Three outline levels with a paragraph under each. The point is the outline rather than the type: a heading that survives as bold text of the right size has lost the thing a table of contents, a navigator and an accessibility tree all read, and it has lost it invisibly. The headings are set in Liberation Sans over a Liberation Serif body because that is the ordinary shape of a document and because it gives the family a second place to be dropped.
seeds.html:
A first level heading

Body text under the first level, so that the heading has something to be a heading of.

A second level heading

Body text under the second level.

A third level heading

Body text under the third level, and the outline is three deep by the time this paragraph is reached.

seeds.why: Both list kinds, each nested one level, with a paragraph on either side. The outer paragraphs are load-bearing - list state must not leak into the prose around it - and the nesting is what separates a format that carries a list from one that carries an indent and a glyph. The expectation asks only for the two prose paragraphs, because whether a list item counts as a paragraph is a question each target answers differently and not one this seed is trying to settle.
seeds.html:
An introductory paragraph, outside every list.

  • first bullet
  • second bullet
    • nested bullet
    • second nested bullet
  • third bullet, back at the outer level
  1. ordered one
  2. ordered two
    1. nested ordered one
    2. nested ordered two

A trailing paragraph, outside every list, because list state must not leak into the prose around it.

textIgnore.why: The generated list label, matched together with the tab that follows it. A bullet glyph and an autonumber come from the list definition rather than from the author, and which target puts one in the text is not a question about the document: DOCX writes a numPr and a numbering part and no glyph anywhere, ODT and HTML write the list structure and no glyph either, and RTF writes the label into the text stream as a {\listtext ...} group carrying the bullet character and a tab. The tab is what makes this safe to match without an anchor, since no seed in this corpus has a tab anywhere in its prose. Without the label the four targets agree about every character the seed actually wrote, and with it they cannot.

seeds.why: Three rows and two columns with a header row, and nothing else - no spans, no nested table, no stated width. A table is the construct where the four targets diverge most and where the divergence is easiest to blame on the wrong thing, so the first table in this corpus is the one with no cell anybody could argue about. The borders are stated because a table that arrives with none looks identical to a table that arrived as paragraphs.
seeds.html:
A paragraph before the table.

head ahead b
cell acell b
cell ccell d

A paragraph after the table.

seeds.why: Two schemes and two positions. example.org is reserved by RFC 2606, so nothing in this corpus names a host anybody owns, and mailto is here because it is the scheme that several writers turn into a field rather than into a hyperlink. The second paragraph puts a link in the middle of a sentence rather than at the start of one, which is where a converter that rebuilds a paragraph around its links gets the surrounding text wrong.
seeds.html:
An absolute link and a mail link and plain text, all in one paragraph.

A paragraph with a second absolute link in the middle of it, so that a link is exercised somewhere other than at a paragraph boundary.

seeds.why: The four alignments and the two indents, one paragraph each. Justify is deliberately long enough to wrap, because a justified single line is set identically to a left aligned one and a short seed would assert nothing at all about the setting it names. The left indent and the first line indent are separate paragraphs because they are separate properties, and a format can carry one of them without the other.
seeds.html:
Left aligned.

Centred.

Right aligned.

Justified, and long enough that justification has something to do with it: a single short line is set identically whether it is justified or left aligned, so a paragraph that did not wrap would say nothing whatever about the alignment it declares, and this one wraps several times before it is finished.

Indented from the left by two centimetres, with no first line indent on top of it.

Indented from the left by two centimetres, with a first line indent of one centimetre as well, because the two are separate properties that a format can carry one of.

seeds.why: The one kind of pagination that does not depend on the host. Where a page breaks because the text ran out is a function of the face, the size and the box; where it breaks because the document said so is a function of the document alone. This is therefore the only seed in the file that can assert a second page without also asserting something about the machine it ran on.
seeds.html:
The paragraph before the break, which is the whole of the first page and nowhere near filling it.

The paragraph after the break, which is the whole of the second page and got there because the document asked rather than because the first page ran out.

seeds.why: The other half of pagination: a flow long enough that the page runs out several times over on any host honouring the stated box and size. The paragraphs are numbered and distinct rather than repeated, so a page that is dropped, duplicated or reordered names itself in the text that comes back instead of hiding in a wall of identical prose. Three pages is asserted as a floor and is far below what this actually fills, because the exact count is a typesetting decision belonging to a program this project does not own.
seeds.html:
Paragraph one of a flow written to be too long for one page. Pagination is the one property in this suite that cannot be asserted from a short document, because where a line breaks depends on the width of the text column and on the metrics of the face that draws it, and where a page breaks depends on how many of those lines fit between the top margin and the bottom one. A seed of three sentences would fill a fraction of a page on every host and would prove nothing about either, so this one is long enough that the page runs out several times over. The count of pages is then a fact about the document rather than a fact about the machine.

Paragraph two exists because a flow of one long paragraph exercises only the break inside a paragraph, and a document breaks between them as well. The two are different code paths in every layout engine worth the name. The first has to decide where a line ends and carry the remainder onto the next one; the second has to decide whether a paragraph starts on the page it was reached on or on the page after it. Widow and orphan control, keep-with-next, and spacing that is dropped at a page boundary all live in the second path, and not one of them can be reached by a document that fits.

Paragraph three, and from here the numbering is doing real work. If a page is dropped, duplicated or reordered, the text that comes back says which one it was. That is worth more than it sounds: a converter that silently truncated a long document would produce a shorter file that read perfectly, and a comparison that asked only whether the text it found was correct would pass it without a word. Asking for the paragraph indices in order asks a harder question, and it is the question a reader who lost the last page of a report would have wanted somebody to ask on their behalf.

Paragraph four. The page box this seed states is 21.59 by 27.94 centimetres with a margin of 2.54 centimetres on every side, which is US Letter with an inch of margin, written in the units the style sheet takes. It is stated rather than inherited because the host locale otherwise decides it, and a locale that chose A4 would give a text column of a different width, a different number of lines to the page and therefore a different number of pages. That difference would look exactly like a defect in the converter, and it would not be one.

Paragraph five. The font is stated for the same reason and with more force, because a missing family is substituted without a word being said anywhere. A document that asked for a face the host does not have is drawn with whatever the host picked instead, and every measurement taken from it afterwards is a measurement of the substitute. The four families this corpus pins are ones a Linux runner and a Windows runner can both be expected to have through the same package, which is a weaker claim than it sounds and is written down here so that nobody has to reconstruct it later from a failing run.

Paragraph six. Nothing in this seed is styled, and that is deliberate rather than lazy. Pagination and inline formatting are separate axes, and a seed that mixed them would fail for two reasons at once and report one of them. The other seeds in this file carry the bold, the colour, the table and the list; this one carries length and nothing else, so that a failure here reads as a failure of the flow and can be taken to the pagination code without a detour through everything else the document might have been asking for.

Paragraph seven. The length is generated rather than repeated. A flow assembled by copying one paragraph twenty times would paginate just as well and would be useless the moment it failed, because every page would look like every other page and the difference would point at all of them equally. Distinct prose costs an afternoon once and pays for itself the first time a converter drops a page from the middle of a document rather than from the end of it, which is the case that is hardest to see and easiest to ship.

Paragraph eight. The line lengths here are ordinary, which is also a choice worth stating. A paragraph made of one very long word cannot be broken by any rule short of hyphenation, and a paragraph of one-letter words breaks anywhere at all; both are interesting and neither is what an author writes. What a document mostly contains is prose of about this shape, and the flow a converter has to get right for the people using it is this one rather than either of the pathological ones.

Paragraph nine. Hyphenation is not switched on, or rather it is not asked for, which is not quite the same thing and is worth naming. A layout engine that hyphenates by default fits more text on a page than one that does not, so two engines can agree about every character of this document and still disagree about how many pages it takes to hold them. That is why the page count is asserted as a floor of three rather than as an equality with whatever number this run happened to produce.

Paragraph ten. A floor is a weaker assertion than an equality and it is the right one here. The purpose of this suite is to catch a document that stopped paginating, not to pin the typesetting decisions of a program this project does not own and cannot fix. Three pages is far below what this flow actually produces on any reasonable host, which leaves room for a version of the office suite that packs its lines a little tighter without anybody being woken up to look at a red build that means nothing.

Paragraph eleven. Half of the flow is behind us, which on most hosts means the second page begins somewhere in this vicinity. Where exactly it begins does not matter and is deliberately written down nowhere: a comment claiming that the break falls after paragraph eleven would be true on the machine it was written on and quietly wrong everywhere else, and the next person to read it would trust it. A fact that only holds on one machine is worse in a comment than it would be in an assertion, because an assertion fails.

Paragraph twelve. The paragraphs here are separated by the style sheet spacing rather than by empty paragraphs between them. An empty paragraph is a paragraph, and a flow padded with them would inflate the paragraph count that this seed expects, so the count would stop meaning what it says it means. The other seeds in this file keep the same discipline for the same reason, and the seed that is actually about empty paragraphs does not exist yet - when it does, it will say so in its own identifier.

Paragraph thirteen. Nothing in this flow contains a character outside Latin-1, which is a restriction this seed accepts and another seed in the file lifts. Encoding and pagination are separate axes too, and a multi-page flow of mixed scripts would be a fine seed for a suite with the time to run it and a poor one for the seed whose only job is to make the page run out. When both fail, two small seeds tell you which of the two broke and one large one does not.

Paragraph fourteen. There is no image, table or list anywhere in this flow either. Each of those changes how a page fills, sometimes dramatically: a table that does not fit is moved or split according to rules that differ between the formats, an image can be larger than the column it sits in, and a list carries indentation that the paragraphs around it do not. Each of them has a seed of its own where the argument about what ought to happen can be had in isolation and settled once.

Paragraph fifteen. What this seed cannot tell you is whether the pages look right. It can say that there are at least three of them, that the text came back in order and complete, and that the page box and the font were the ones that were asked for. Whether the third page begins where a typesetter would have begun it is a judgement, and a suite that pretended to make that judgement would in fact be asserting the preferences of whoever wrote the assertion, on every host, for ever.

Paragraph sixteen. It also cannot tell you that the documents it produced are readable by anything other than the program that wrote them. Every target here is written by one office suite and read back by the same one, which is a real limitation and the reason this file sits beside the corpus that goes through this component's own codecs rather than replacing it. Agreement between two implementations is evidence about a format; agreement of a program with itself is a smaller and more comfortable thing.

Paragraph seventeen. The seed is authored as HTML because HTML is the one input format that can be written as a string in a manifest, read by the office suite without a converter of this project's own standing in the way, and reviewed by a person looking at the file in a diff. A binary seed would have had to be committed, and no document of a supported format is committed in this repository, which is a rule with a guard behind it rather than a habit.

Paragraph eighteen. That rule is enforced rather than remembered. A guard walks the whole tree and fails the build if a file with one of the reading extensions appears anywhere in it, which is exactly why this corpus states markup and manufactures its documents in a temporary workspace on every run instead. The workspace is thrown away when the run ends, so the only durable artefact of a run is the report it printed, and the documents themselves are reproducible from this file by anybody.

Paragraph nineteen. The flow has by now passed whatever a reasonable page can hold, twice over, on any host that honours the stated box and the stated size, which is the property this seed was written for and the only one it claims. The paragraphs that follow are here for margin rather than for coverage, because a seed that only just reached its floor would start failing on the first host that set its lines a little tighter than the host it was written on.

Paragraph twenty. Margin is cheap in a file like this and expensive to add later, once a run has gone red on somebody else's machine for a reason nobody can reproduce on their own. A seed sized to just clear its own assertion is a seed that will need somebody's afternoon eventually. This one is sized to clear it several times over, which costs a few thousand characters in a manifest that is already read by a machine rather than by a person in a hurry.

Paragraph twenty-one. There is a second reason for the volume, and it is the one that made the length worth writing rather than generating. A converter that loses text tends to lose it at a boundary - the end of a page, the end of a section, the end of a buffer - and a flow with many boundaries offers many chances to catch that. A short document has one boundary, and a converter can be wrong at every boundary it has and still produce a document that reads perfectly.

Paragraph twenty-two. The paragraphs are all of roughly the same length, which is neither deliberate nor load-bearing. A flow of wildly uneven paragraphs would exercise the page break decision more sharply, because a very long paragraph arriving near the bottom of a page is where keep-with-next and orphan control actually have something to decide. That would be a better seed than this one for that particular question, and it would be a worse seed for this one, which is about volume.

Paragraph twenty-three. Two more and this flow is finished. It is worth saying plainly that none of this prose is documentation of the office suite, of any format, or of this component: it is ballast with the useful property of being distinguishable from itself. If it ever needs to be replaced with something shorter and denser that fills the same number of pages, nothing anywhere depends on a word of it beyond the paragraph numbers and the count.

Paragraph twenty-four. A word about the office suite itself, since it is the one part of this arrangement that nobody here controls. It is found rather than assumed: the runner looks where its own configuration says it should be, then at the places the platform installs it, and if neither of those finds it then the whole group of checks is a skip that names the paths it looked at. It is never an exception and it is never a silent pass, because a suite that quietly stopped running half of itself reads exactly like a suite that passed.

Paragraph twenty-five. That distinction matters more here than in most of this repository, because the office suite is a large program that is present on a developer's machine and frequently absent from a container. A run that failed on its absence would be a run everybody learned to ignore within a week; a run that passed on its absence would be a run that proved nothing while claiming otherwise. A skip with a reason, printed next to the pass and fail counts, is the only one of the three that a person can act on.

Paragraph twenty-six. The workspace is a temporary directory chosen by the operating system rather than by this project, which is a small decision with a reason behind it. A path this project picked would be a path this project has to clean up, and a run interrupted halfway would leave a document of a supported format sitting in a tree that a guard walks and fails the build over. Letting the platform choose keeps the guard's job simple and keeps the interrupted run harmless.

Paragraph twenty-seven. Every document this suite measures is therefore written and destroyed inside a single run, and not one of them can be looked at afterwards - only reproduced from this file. That is a real cost when a failure is hard to read, and the answer to it is not to start keeping the documents but to print the command that made them, so that a person can produce the same document by hand and open it in the program that wrote it.

Paragraph twenty-eight. On the subject of what a run ought to print: the report names the seed, then the target, then the check, in that order, because that is the order in which a person narrows down a failure. Knowing that something went wrong in the DOCX conversion is less useful than knowing that the table seed went wrong in the DOCX conversion, and which of the two it was is not a question anybody can answer from a count of failures.

Paragraph twenty-nine. It is worth saying plainly what this whole file is not. It is not a claim that any of the four target formats has been implemented correctly by anybody, this component included. It is a claim about agreement: that a document written by one program and read back by another says the same thing at both ends. Agreement is weaker than correctness, and it is the strongest thing a suite with no reference implementation to compare against can honestly assert.

Paragraph thirty. The seeds around this one are each about a single construct, and the reason bears repeating in the one seed that is not about a construct at all. A seed exercising a table and a colour and a nested list would fail whenever any of the three broke, and the report would say only that the seed failed. Somebody would open it, read three constructs and guess. Twelve small seeds cost twelve identifiers and answer the question the report was asked.

Paragraph thirty-one. Several constructs are missing from the twelve, and their absence is a decision rather than an oversight: footnotes, headers and footers, fields, comments, tracked changes, embedded images and sections. Each is a real thing that real documents contain, and each needs a seed of its own with an argument attached to it. They arrive when somebody has that argument, and until then this file says what it covers by covering it and nothing else.

Paragraph thirty-two. Images in particular are absent for a reason that belongs here rather than in a comment nobody will read. An image seed needs image bytes, and image bytes in a manifest are either an enormous string or a file on disk that a guard would object to. The other corpus in this repository solved that by rendering its own fixture with the tool under test, which was available to it and is not available here, because the tool under test in this file is an office suite.

Paragraph thirty-three. The flow is long by now, and it is worth naming what the length is buying, because a reader skimming this file will reasonably wonder whether it is padding. It is padding, and it is the useful kind. A page count cannot be asserted without pages, pages cannot be produced without text, and text that repeats itself makes a dropped page invisible, so every sentence here is doing the only job a sentence can do in a seed like this one.

Paragraph thirty-four. Two paragraphs left. If a converter has carried this seed intact as far as here, it has moved something on the order of twenty thousand characters across a format boundary without dropping, duplicating or reordering any of them. That is a stronger statement than any of the short seeds in this file can make on its own, and a weaker one than it sounds, because not one of those characters was in any way difficult.

Paragraph thirty-five. The difficult characters live in the seed about scripts and the seed about entities, where a converter that handles this entire flow without a fault may still lose a soft hyphen or a direction. Length and difficulty are separate axes, which is the same argument this file makes about every other pair of properties it touches, and it holds here for the last time before the flow ends.

Paragraph thirty-six, and the last. If this paragraph is missing from what a target read back, then the converter lost the end of the document, which is the failure this seed is best at finding and the one a person reading the output would notice last of all. Everything above it is the flow; this sentence is the marker that says the flow arrived whole.

seeds.why: Four scripts and a direction. The body is set in DejaVu Sans because it is the only pinned family covering Greek, Cyrillic and Hebrew, and the CJK line is here in the knowledge that no pinned family covers it at all - that line is evidence about text and about nothing else, and saying so is better than letting a pixel comparison quietly measure whatever the host substituted. The last paragraph puts a right-to-left run inside a left-to-right sentence, which is the case a paragraph-level direction property cannot express. The ignore list is empty on purpose and the obvious candidate was rejected on evidence: an invisible bidirectional formatting character wrapped around the run would have been worth ignoring, and no target writes one - HTML states the direction as an attribute and RTF as a control word - so an ignore would silence a difference that does not happen and would be the wrong way round on the day one started. It is the one seed that declares substitutesFonts, because it deliberately asks for glyphs no pinned family has: the font guard would otherwise report LibreOffice picking a CJK face as a failure, when picking one is the only thing it could have done.
seeds.html:
Latin with diacritics, as a control: café, naïve, Fußball.

Greek: Καλημέρα κόσμε, και μια δεύτερη πρόταση.

Cyrillic: Привет, мир, и второе предложение здесь.

CJK: 你好世界 こんにちは世界 안녕하세요 세계.

עברית: שלום עולם, ומשפט שני.

A Latin lead-in, then a right-to-left run in the middle of the sentence - العربية: مرحبا بالعالم - and then Latin again after it.

seeds.why: The characters a format has to make a decision about rather than simply carry. The doubled space is held open by white-space:pre-wrap and drawn in a monospaced face, because HTML collapses it otherwise and a seed that lost the construct in its own source would be testing nothing at all. The non-breaking space, the soft hyphen, the ampersand and the less-than are each written twice, once as a named entity and once as a numeric reference, so a reader that handles one spelling and not the other is caught by the two paragraphs disagreeing rather than by both being wrong together.
seeds.html:
Two literal spaces sit between the words gap here, held open by white-space:pre-wrap and drawn in a monospaced face so that a person reading the output can see them.

Named entities: a non-breaking space, a soft­hyphen inside a word, an ampersand & and a less-than < sign.

The same four as numeric references: a non-breaking space, a soft­hyphen inside a word, an ampersand & and a less-than < sign.

textIgnore.why: The soft hyphen, and only that character. It is a discretionary break rather than text: DOCX carries it as an element of its own, RTF as a control word, ODT and HTML as the character itself, and what an extractor hands back for the first two is the extractor's choice rather than the document's. Removing it before comparing keeps this seed asserting that the word around it survived intact, and leaves whether the break itself survived to a check that can tell an absent soft hyphen from an unextracted one - which a text comparison cannot.

seeds.why:
A forced line break inside a paragraph. Every one of the four targets has a way to write one - text:line-break, w:br, \line,
- and no other seed here contains a single one, which is an omission rather than a ceiling:
is plain HTML and nobody had used it. The first block is an address because that is the shape the construct takes in a real document, and because five short lines make the failure unmistakable. Each is short enough that two would fit on one line of this column, so a break that arrives as an ordinary space does not move a word, it collapses the block and lifts everything after it up the page. The assertion is a pixel one and the seed says so rather than implying otherwise: the text canonicalisation maps a line separator to a newline on both sides before comparing, so `text` cannot tell a break that was honoured from one that was not, and only the render can. The paragraph floor stays at three, because a break is not a paragraph and a target that made it one would itself be the finding.
seeds.html:
Sender Name
Broiler Platform
12 Example Street
00000 Example City
Example State

A break is not a paragraph, and this one proves it twice:
a second line,
and a third.

Every line above is short enough that two of them would fit on one line of this column, so a break that arrives as an ordinary space does not merely move a word - it collapses the block, and the paragraph after it moves up the page by four lines. That is the whole assertion of this seed, and it is a pixel one: a text projection turns a line separator into a newline on both sides before comparing, so no comparison of text can tell the two apart.

seeds.why: The letterhead: a gradient-filled band anchored in the first page's header, a bordered box carrying its own text anchored in the body and stacked in front of the band, a footer with a page number in it, and a master page that names the one that follows it. This is the first seed written in flat ODF, and it is the reason that form exists. LibreOffice's HTML import manufactures none of these, which was measured rather than assumed: across the twenty-four ODT and DOCX documents the html seeds produce there is not one header, footer, anchored frame, shape fill or field, so a difference in any of them could not fail this suite, because no document in it had one. It carries more than one construct, against this file's usual rule, and that is the point rather than an exception to it: what it exists to ask is which of two frames is drawn on top, and stacking cannot be asked of either frame alone. The band is in the header and the box is in the body because that is the pairing a letterhead makes, and the one where the answer is least obvious. Three choices inside it were made against a specific alternative. The gradient states its angle as 30deg rather than as unitless tenths of a degree, because that is what LibreOffice 24.2 writes; a reader that understood only the older spelling would treat the attribute as absent and draw the band the wrong way round, and silently, since a failed parse and a missing attribute reach the same branch. Page two is reached by an explicit break rather than by overflowing, so multipage is a fact about the document and not about the host's font metrics - the rule page-break-explicit already follows. And there is a second page at all so that the master-page chain has something to be wrong about: the band belongs to the first page and the page number to every page after it, and a reader that stopped at the first master page would put the band on both and the number on neither. The html target is the weak one and is kept anyway. LibreOffice flattens both frames to GIF files beside the document, so that row measures a raster where the other three measure a frame. A row recording that is worth more than a target quietly absent from the corpus.

text:style-name="pCentred">BADGE</text:p></draw:text-box></draw:frame>The band down the left margin is a gradient-filled frame anchored in the header of the first page. The bordered box over it is a second frame anchored in this paragraph, and the document stacks it in front of the band.</text:p><text:p>Neither frame is reachable from HTML, which is why this seed is written in flat ODF.
